Today it is a branch shrine administered by nearby {{ill|Kinomiya Shrine|Q11523682|qid=Q11523682}}, and goshuin can be received at Kinomiya Shrine.

=== Enshrined deity ===
The shrine enshrines {{ill|Beauty and the Beast (1991 soundtrack)|Q849233|qid=Q849233|lt=Sukunahikona-no-Kami}}. Although Sukunahikona is worshiped nationwide in {{ill|Japan|Q17|qid=Q17}} as a deity of hot springs, this shrine is thought originally to have worshiped the Oyū spring itself as a deity.<ref>"Shikinaisha Chosa Hokoku."</ref>

=== Origin and history ===
According to shrine tradition, in June 749 (Tenpyo-shoho 1), a divine oracle was delivered to a child instructing that hot-spring water should be drawn and used for bathing because it would cure illnesses; local residents then built a small shrine and enshrined Sukunahikona in gratitude.<ref>"Tokusen Jinmeicho," citing "Atami Onsen-ki."</ref>

Another tradition says that in the mid-8th century, the monk Mangan Shonin, who had resided at Kongooin on Mt. Hakone, pitied the fish and shellfish dying from boiling spring water emerging in Atami's sea. After 100 days of prayer on a ritual platform by the shore, the spring vein shifted inland on the final day, and the deity came to be worshiped there as "Yuzen Gongen," guardian deity of the hot spring.<ref>"Yuzen Gongen Haiden Saiko Kanjincho" dated 1667 (Atami City Library collection).</ref>

The shrine is identified with "Atami no Yu Myojin" in the Tagata-gun section of the ''Izu no Kuni Shinkaicho'', and the "Onsen-jinshi" mentioned in the ''Genko Shakusho'' is also inferred to refer to this shrine.<ref name="shizuoka-place">"Shizuoka-ken no Chimei."</ref> There is also a theory identifying it with "Kuzumi Shrine" in the ''Engishiki Jinmyocho''. In the medieval period and later it was widely called "Yuzen Gongen," and as devotion to the two gongen of Izusan (Hashiriyu) and Hakone spread among shoguns and Kamakura shogunate elites from the {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}}, it was broadly promoted as a deity of hot-spring healing.<ref name="shizuoka-place"/>

=== Rituals ===
;Atami Yu Festival (February and October)
: The spring and autumn grand festivals.
: Based on the old custom of presenting Atami hot-spring water to {{ill|Edo Castle|Q865913|qid=Q865913}} in the Edo period, the first day of the autumn festival includes a "Yukumi-dochu" parade in which participants carry buckets of hot-spring water.<ref name="izu2013106">{{Cite news
  | title = "Yukumi-dochu" held in grand style as Yuzen Shrine grand festival opens
  | newspaper = {{ill|Izu Shimbun|Q11380576|qid=Q11380576}}
  | publisher = Izu Shimbun
  | date = 2013-10-06
}}</ref>
: On the second day, the "Kento-sai" is performed, offering hot-spring water from Oyū before the deity.<ref name="izu2013106"/>

=== Precinct ===
* {{ill|Camphora officinarum|Q158722|qid=Q158722}}
: About half of the trunk is fire-damaged, but the tree remains vigorous; height 17 m, trunk circumference 7.2 m (at the time of Atami City natural monument designation).<ref name=":1">On-site guide board installed by the Atami City Board of Education.</ref>
* Stone torii
: Donated in 1780 (An'ei 9) when the 7th lord of the {{ill|Kurume Domain|Q426826|qid=Q426826}}, {{ill|Arima Yoriyuki|Q3135437|qid=Q3135437}}, visited Atami. The stone of both pillars is hollowed. Height 3.45 m, width 4.1 m, pillar diameter 0.35 m. The donation year is engraved on the pillars.<ref name=":2">On-site guide board installed by the Yuzen Shrine support association.</ref>
* Stone lanterns
: Donated in 1758 (Horeki 8) by Arima Yoritaka when he visited Atami. Height 2.05 m, pillar diameter 0.35 m. The donation year is engraved on the pillar.<ref name=":2"/>
* Temizu basin
: Spring water formerly flowed here, but it is currently stopped.
* Haiden and honden
